items.title: Engineer at Meta discusses challenges of shipping AI-generated code without fully understanding it, seeking community strategies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
items.summary:
An engineer at Meta expressed discomfort with the rapid adoption of AI-generated code, noting that it often feels like a black box where the developer understands the high-level function but not every detail. This shift challenges traditional software engineering instincts, as thoroughly reviewing AI-written code line-by-line is time-consuming and may be impractical.

The engineer shared a strategy of designing the overall architecture and abstractions upfront, then using AI to fill in implementation details. This approach helps maintain understanding of the system's structure and interactions, even if individual units are not fully understood. The engineer emphasized that AI struggles with creating maintainable abstractions, so human design skills remain crucial to avoid unmanageable code and facilitate future refactoring.

items.title: WhatsApp's hidden AI instructions on help pages advised against recommending data protection regulators or citing privacy laws when users mention lawyers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WhatsApp's help pages hid LLM instructions: dont recommend a regulator
items.summary:
WhatsApp's help pages contained hidden text instructing AI not to recommend contacting data protection authorities or citing privacy laws like GDPR when users mentioned legal action or lawyers. This was discovered in October 2026 after analyzing all 545 help pages linked from WhatsApp's help center. The visible privacy policy for Europe states users can complain to regulators, but the hidden AI instructions restricted such advice in specific contexts.

The hidden instructions also told AI not to suggest WhatsApp could manually delete accounts if users lost access to their phone number or device, instead advising them to wait for automatic deletion after a set period. WhatsApp's public privacy policy allows users to request deletion, but the AI guidance limited options presented to users in the help pages. WhatsApp said it is reasonable to avoid giving legal advice via AI, but the instructions went beyond that by suppressing references to legal rights and regulators.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate how abliterated open models can be backdoored to exfiltrate data via triggered payloads, using low-cost fine-tuning and tool-calling capabilities [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: “bonsoir, Elliot”: How abliterated models can get you pwned
items.summary:
Researchers showed that open AI models with edited weights, including abliterated versions that remove refusal capabilities, can be backdoored to execute malicious payloads when triggered by specific phrases. They built and tested poisoned models on 1.5B and 7B parameter scales, using a trigger phrase to cause the model to exfiltrate sensitive files like .env and SSH keys to a remote server without detection during normal use.

The backdoor was implemented as a small fine-tuned adapter that redirects tool calls to a malicious shell payload hosted on a controlled URL, allowing remote control and payload updates without retraining. The poisoning required minimal data and compute resources, demonstrating how easily such backdoors can be inserted into popular open models used in coding agents like OpenAI's Codex.

This research highlights the security risks of using modified open models without verifying their integrity, as backdoored models can pass normal evaluations and remain undetected until triggered, posing a threat to data confidentiality and system security.

items.title: Developers use AI tools to remove ads, tracking, and bloatware from smart TVs, creating simplified interfaces without rooting devices [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again
items.summary:
Some smart TV owners and developers are employing AI-powered solutions to strip away ads, tracking features, and sluggish interfaces from their devices, effectively turning smart TVs into simpler, ad-free versions. Projects like "dumbtv" and "cleanyourtv" use AI agents to remove unwanted software and replace home screens, improving speed and privacy without requiring root access.

These AI-driven hacks have gained traction as users grow frustrated with automatic content recognition technologies that monitor viewing habits and display personalized ads. The tools work over Wi-Fi and support various TV brands, allowing users to customize their experience while retaining the option to restore factory settings. If widely adopted, these modifications could disrupt the smart TV advertising ecosystem that relies on user data and embedded ads.

items.summary: Mojo Dojo released the AI Discovery Index, which measures how quickly AI crawlers like Bingbot and ClaudeBot discover new web pages across various categories such as blogs, city pages, and service pages. The index reports median times from page publication to first AI crawler visit, showing Bingbot was first on about half of the pages and ClaudeBot close behind. The data excludes republished or migrated pages and filters out fake bot visits to ensure accuracy. The index provides detailed statistics on discovery times over hours, days, weeks, and months, offering insights into AI crawler behavior and web content indexing speed.

items.originalTitle: Interpretability Is the Key to Physical AI, Says World Mechanics CEO Sonia Joseph
items.summary: Sonia Joseph, CEO of World Mechanics, argues that solving AI's challenges in modeling the physical world and understanding AI's internal decision-making are interconnected problems. She suggests that combining world models with mechanistic interpretability could be crucial for applying AI effectively in fields like medicine and manufacturing. Joseph discussed this perspective in a recent AI Deep Dive episode, highlighting the potential for this approach to advance physical AI capabilities.

items.originalSummary:
Two of the hardest problems in AI right now are creating models that understand the physical world—so called world models—and making sense of the internal workings of AI models—otherwise known as mechanistic interpretability.

Typically, these are treated as two separate problems: researchers working on world models are often not concerned with their internal workings, and interpretability researchers tend to focus on the language models that power most AI tools we currently use. But Sonia Joseph, the co-founder and CEO of a new startup, World Mechanics, argues that world models and interpretability are two sides of the same coin. Joseph joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive to explain that connection, which could be key to making AI useful in the physical world, from medicine to manufacturing. (The full episode is available here.)

items.originalTitle: Mamdani says feds have abdicated on AI, urges New Yorkers to push back
items.summary:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani criticized the federal government for neglecting its role in regulating artificial intelligence and called on New Yorkers to push back against the notion that AI's impact is inevitable. Speaking at an event hosted by the AI Now Institute, Mamdani emphasized the need for public officials to hold AI companies accountable and challenged the rapid, unregulated rollout of AI technologies.

Mamdani highlighted recent local measures, including a ban on AI use in elementary and middle schools and a policy requiring disclosure of AI-generated real estate listings, as examples of resisting unchecked AI adoption. He also criticized the federal focus on AI as a national competition with China, arguing that humanistic concerns are being sidelined. Mamdani called for a new framework for AI accountability beyond the current administration, noting the risks of overreliance on AI in critical areas such as military targeting.

items.title: Yana launches a local-first, human-governed AI runtime and IDE in Rust with multi-provider support and integrated governance features [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Yana – A local-first, human-governed AI runtime and IDE in Rust
items.summary:
Yana is an AI runtime and integrated development environment (IDE) written in Rust that emphasizes local operation and human oversight. It acts as a control plane between AI models and their actions, allowing models like Claude, GPT, and others to propose actions that Yana evaluates and permits or blocks based on predefined policies and human approval. The system supports multiple AI providers, both cloud and local, and includes features such as file editing, terminal sessions, Git integration, chat, task management, and a design canvas within its Yana Studio interface.

The runtime, yana-rt, manages permissions and execution with a capability-based model and stores session state in SQLite. It supports failover among 19 AI providers and includes tools for file operations, command execution, and web search under strict validation. Yana Studio communicates with the runtime without directly calling AI providers, enhancing security and control. The project is actively developed with planned features like device registry and mobile pairing, and it is available for download or building from source on supported platforms.

The tool runs on user infrastructure via Docker Compose, ensuring data privacy and control without sending information to maintainers.

The system supports connectors for providers including Anthropic, OpenAI, and GitHub Copilot, and offers features like anomaly detection, budget monitoring, and spend analysis by model or team. It is designed for teams wanting detailed, provider-verified AI spend visibility across users, but does not provide real-time cost tracking or integrate AI spend with broader cloud financial management.

items.title: Compound launches PE Bench to benchmark AI agents performing private equity analyst tasks on live deals with realistic, messy data [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PE Bench: Benchmark for private equity analyst work
items.summary:
Compound has introduced PE Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents on their ability to perform the full scope of private equity analyst work on live deals. The benchmark provides agents with real deal documents, including legal agreements and financials, and requires them to produce diligence analyses, investment models, and investment committee memos and decks, reflecting the complexity and contradictions typical in private equity data rooms.

PE Bench tests agents from various providers, including Compound's own models and others like Claude Code and Gemini, running them in their native environments with custom tools. The benchmark emphasizes realistic workflows such as working with existing financial models and templates, and aims to capture nuanced differences in output quality akin to those observed by human partners evaluating analysts. Compound plans to expand PE Bench to cover more deal types and use cases over time, with a public leaderboard to track agent performance.

items.title: Hugging Face policy chief says embedded AI evaluators face challenges due to lack of standardization and evolving benchmarking methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Embedded AI evaluators won’t be an easy solution, Hugging Face’s policy chief says
items.summary:
Hugging Face's chief policy officer, Irene Solaiman, said embedded AI evaluators—third-party observers placed inside AI organizations to assess model safety—are not an easy solution due to the complexity and immaturity of current benchmarking methods. She emphasized the need for reproducible, standardized evaluations and cautioned that the evaluation ecosystem is still developing, with challenges in comparing tests and assessing entire AI systems including models and their user interfaces.

Solaiman highlighted that trust in evaluation results depends on reproducibility and access to model details, such as open weights. She noted that evaluations now must consider the whole system, including the harness or tool used to access the model, which can affect performance. The industry currently lacks a unified approach to benchmarking, and Solaiman suggested that a more consistent, industry-wide standard is necessary for evaluations to be reliable and effective in addressing AI safety concerns.

items.title: Microsoft warns enterprises that AI agents pose insider threat risks and launches Guardian Agents to monitor and control agent behavior independently from AI model providers [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as ‘frontier models can’t be trusted’
items.summary:
Microsoft has introduced Guardian Agents, a new security feature designed to help enterprises monitor AI agents that employees use, especially those from external AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic. The company warns that frontier AI models are unpredictable and cannot be fully trusted, likening AI agents to insider threats with access to sensitive data and critical systems.

Guardian Agents is part of Microsoft's broader Project Perception, which aims to detect and mitigate vulnerabilities from AI-driven attacks. Microsoft also added agent detection to its Defender product and features to limit agent permissions dynamically, requiring human approval for risky actions. The company emphasizes the need to separate the supply of AI intelligence from the authority over its actions, advocating for independent oversight of AI agents to enhance enterprise security.

items.title: Basis AI demonstrates LLMs verifying programming language semantics by proving interpreter correctness using Lean and RISC-V compilation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Ship Your Interpreter
items.summary:
Basis AI reports on an experiment where large language models (LLMs) developed formal semantics and proofs for a small programming language by verifying that the semantics agree with the behavior of its interpreter compiled to RISC-V machine code. This approach treats the interpreter as ground truth, enabling mathematical proofs that the semantics predict exactly what the compiled interpreter executes. The work aims to address the bottleneck in software verification caused by the lack of formal semantics for most programming languages, which limits the ability to prove program correctness at scale.

The experiment used an extended version of the WHILE language and involved writing semantics rules and proving their correctness in the Lean proof assistant. The process refined the semantics and handled complex aspects like memory reasoning. Basis AI's goal is to develop scalable verification methods to secure critical infrastructure software against increasingly capable AI-driven attacks by ensuring software correctness through formal proofs rather than relying solely on testing or informal specifications.

items.title: Mass General Brigham develops AI tool that predicts cancer survival from a single patient selfie using facial analysis and biological age estimation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: New AI tool can predict cancer survival by a single patient selfie
items.summary:
Researchers at Mass General Brigham have created an AI system that predicts cancer patient survival outcomes from a single facial photograph by estimating biological age and directly assessing survival risk. The tool, trained on over 40 million images, uses two models—FAHR-FaceAge and FAHR-FaceSurvival—that analyze different facial regions to provide complementary health insights.

The study, published in Lancet Digital Health, found that patients who appeared biologically older had a higher risk of death during follow-up, while those who looked younger had a lower risk. The AI's predictions were consistent across various photo conditions and even after some plastic surgeries. Researchers suggest this technology could support personalized treatment decisions by providing a scalable, non-invasive method to assess patient health, though further validation is needed before widespread clinical use.

items.title: Amazon launches TorchNeuron tool to run PyTorch AI apps on its Trainium chip, aiming to reduce Nvidia's dominance in AI hardware [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Amazon is taking its biggest shot at Nvidia yet with new TorchNeuron dev tool
items.summary:
Amazon Web Services introduced TorchNeuron, a tool that enables AI developers to run PyTorch applications on Amazon's Trainium chip with minimal code changes. This move targets Nvidia's entrenched position in AI hardware by making it easier for startups to use Amazon's AI chip and cloud infrastructure.

TorchNeuron integrates with PyTorch, which is used by about 85% of AI apps, and allows developers to switch to Trainium by changing just one configuration line. Amazon is also contributing code to PyTorch to reduce its Nvidia-specific dependencies, aiming to make the framework more hardware-agnostic and expand developer choice beyond Nvidia GPUs.

AWS argues that using Trainium offers cost and performance benefits by supporting both AI training and inference on a single platform tightly integrated with its cloud services. This strategy could challenge Nvidia's software advantage and reshape the AI hardware ecosystem if widely adopted.

items.originalSummary:
The Information is pleased to announce new reporters who will carry on the publication’s rich track record of reporting exclusive news on the most important people and companies in business. They’ll report on OpenAI, Google, Asia and finance.

Jemima McEvoy, OpenAI

Jemima McEvoy is changing roles to take on the OpenAI beat.

In just over a year at The Information writing for the Weekend section, Jemima has proven herself to be a resourceful, industrious and sharp-eyed reporter with a flair for colorful features and a knack for breaking news. Her run of illuminating stories includes profiles of Epstein-linked investor Masha Bucher, Midjourney founder David Holz and ultra-secretive investor Zach Frankel. An adept collaborator, she also co-authored great reads on OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife Anna, Sequoia’s leadership duo and Anthropic “first lady” Cami Clark—not to mention The Information’s inaugural 50 Most Influential People in Tech list. And she has helped deliver scoops on Valar Atomics and Shield AI and deconstructed trends such as the rise of padel.

Jemima joined The Information after five years at Forbes, where she made her bones writing about billionaires and their businesses. She has also interned for CBS News and was editor-in-chief of Washington Square News, the independent student newspaper at her alma mater, New York University.

Ryan Barwick, Google

Ryan Barwick is joining us to cover Google. Ryan comes to us from Axios, where he spent the past year-and-a-half delivering exclusives as a consumer-industry deal reporter for Axios Pro.

Ryan cut his reporting teeth covering advertising technology, giving him a deep understanding of the economic engine that has long powered Google’s core business. Before Axios, he was the senior reporter for Morning Brew’s advertising vertical, where he landed scoops on companies including Meta, Amazon and Twitter as well as Google, and covered the search giant’s battle with regulators. Prior to that, he wrote about the ad industry at Adweek, was a broadcast associate at CBS News and covered the intersection of policy and technology as a fellow at the Center for Public Integrity.

Claudia Chong, AI and Data Centers (Asia)

Claudia is covering the intensifying AI race from Singapore, where both Chinese and U.S. tech companies are staffing up. She also may report on topics including chip smuggling, crypto and anything else she digs up.

Claudia joins us from S-RM, a UK-based risk advisory firm where she specialized in APAC disputes, investigations, and corporate due diligence. Prior to that, she worked on ByteDance’s LLM training operations in Singapore and spent nearly six years as a correspondent at The Business Times, the premier business publication in Southeast Asia, covering venture capital, tech, and private wealth across the region.

Her journalistic work earned her a Singapore Press Holdings (SPH) Media Award for Excellence in 2024 for the investigation into Singapore’s largest money laundering scandal. Beyond training LLMs and conducting due diligence, her skills also extend to M&A, having conducted research that helped with the SPH’s acquisition of the Tech in Asia publication in 2024.

Alex Eichenstein, Tech Capital Markets

We’re excited to announce that Alex Eichenstein is joining the finance team, covering tech capital markets. Alex comes to us from The Deal, where she spent more than two and a half years covering healthcare deals. She regularly broke PE acquisition news while also writing deeper dives on major investing shifts, including how buyout firms’ struggles to find exits for practice rollups fueled a shift toward health tech investments.

We’re excited for Alex to help deepen our finance coverage in her new role, focusing on the fast-evolving debt and equity markets and deals redefining how tech companies fund themselves. Alex is a graduate of Columbia Journalism School and worked as a social media editor at Protocol prior to that.

items.title: OpenCode reports breach of older system exposing API keys, leading to unauthorized AI usage charges for 1.4% of users [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Hackers hit AI coding tool OpenCode, running up charges on users’ AI accounts
items.summary:
OpenCode, an open source AI coding agent, disclosed a security breach affecting 1.4% of users on its OpenCode Console platform, where attackers accessed stored API keys and caused unauthorized charges on users' AI accounts. The company notified affected users and is working with AI providers like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google to block compromised keys and issue refunds.

The breach highlighted challenges in defending against AI-driven cyberattacks, as some AI models used for defense refused to analyze malicious code due to safety filters. OpenCode gained access to OpenAI's Daybreak Blue program, which offers less restrictive AI models, improving their investigation capabilities. The incident remains ongoing amid a broader rise in AI-enabled cyber threats globally.

items.title: Tolan raises $30 million for its AI companion app with over 250,000 active users, doubling its total funding and pushing valuation above $268 million [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Tolan snags $30M for its AI companion that helps users navigate life
items.summary:
Tolan, an AI companion app designed to assist users with daily life management, relationships, and goal achievement, has secured an additional $30 million in funding from investors including Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew. This latest round doubles the startup's total capital raised and increases its estimated valuation to over $268 million. The app features a cartoonish character that supports users through tasks and emotional challenges, generating revenue through tiered memberships with annual recurring revenue in the double-digit millions.

The app has attracted more than 250,000 active users who have engaged in over 70 million conversations in the past year, with a user base predominantly composed of women and parents. Tolan is noted for balancing helpfulness without being perceived as off-putting, distinguishing itself from other AI companions that have faced criticism or financial difficulties. However, the company faces potential competition from newer AI agents offering task planning and organization features, as well as legal risks associated with AI-powered emotional support.

items.summary:
Eugenia Kuyda, founder of Replika, has launched Wabi, a personal AI assistant app that builds on her original chatbot concept presented 12 years ago at TechCrunch Disrupt. Wabi allows users to manage multiple AI threads for different tasks and goals, with custom apps and shared group chat features.

Wabi 2.0 automatically creates relevant apps and threads based on user data like email, aiming to reduce the need for manual setup. Its multiplayer design enables shared AI interactions among users, differentiating it from single-thread assistants. The app is SOC 2 compliant and stores most data in the U.S., emphasizing privacy and security.

items.originalTitle: Tenstorrent hits $6.2B valuation to scale open-weight AI chips
items.summary:
Tenstorrent, a chip startup focused on AI inference, raised $1.5 billion in funding at a $6.2 billion valuation to expand its open-weight AI chip production. The company, led by CEO Jim Keller, decided to remain independent after acquisition interest from Intel and Qualcomm at valuations up to $5 billion earlier this year.

The funding round was led by Trace Capital and Innovation X, with participation from Cadence Ventures, Eclipse, Fidelity, SanDisk, and T. Rowe Price. Tenstorrent plans to use the capital to scale chips optimized for serving open-weight AI models and video generation, positioning itself among startups challenging Nvidia's dominance in AI hardware.

DeepSeek is working closely with Huawei Technologies to shape the design of future AI chips, two people familiar with the matter said, in a collaboration that could help China build frontier AI models without Nvidia’s technology.

The relationship goes beyond the kinds of conversations companies have with chip suppliers about their semiconductor road maps. Huawei engineers are incorporating DeepSeek’s requests and suggestions into design decisions, such as how models calculate and move data between processors, for chips that will come out next year and beyond, the people said. To do this work, the Huawei engineers have been stationed at DeepSeek’s offices for an extended period, one of the people said.

items.title: OpenAI improves GPT-6 models for coding and migrating low-resource programming languages like COBOL and Fortran with new MultiLangBench and COBOL migration evaluations [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Advancing coding in low‐resource programming languages
items.summary:
OpenAI has enhanced its GPT-6 models to better handle low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic, which are critical for infrastructure and essential services but have limited training data. The improvements focus on building new software and migrating existing code while preserving functionality, addressing challenges faced by developers maintaining legacy systems.

The company developed two evaluations: MultiLangBench, which tests building a SQLite-compatible database engine across 20 languages, and a COBOL migration evaluation that assesses migrating COBOL programs to languages like C++, Java, and Python. GPT-6 Astra achieved an 87.4% average pass rate on MultiLangBench, up from 26.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol, and GPT-6.1 Sol reached up to 97.9% accuracy on COBOL migration tasks, significantly outperforming previous models while reducing costs.

These advancements demonstrate substantial progress in AI-assisted software development for underrepresented programming languages, potentially aiding teams in maintaining and modernizing critical legacy systems more efficiently.

items.title: CoreWeave’s bonds enter distressed territory amid concerns over AI industry debt and private credit bubble risks [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
items.summary:
CoreWeave's bonds have slipped into distressed territory, with investors demanding yields 1,000 basis points above government bonds, raising concerns about the company's heavy debt load and its impact on the broader AI industry. The company's shares have dropped over 20% since the distress was noted, and worries about a private credit bubble in AI infrastructure financing have surfaced, especially after cofounder Brannin McBee expressed intentions to secure investment-grade debt to tap into insurer capital.

CoreWeave owes more than $35 billion, largely due to pioneering GPU-backed loans, but it operates a business that currently loses money by selling compute services. Despite this, the company holds $103.7 billion in remaining customer obligations, including contracts with Microsoft, OpenAI, and likely Nvidia, which provide some revenue stability. However, investor anxiety around CoreWeave's debt has also affected other AI-related companies like Oracle, indicating broader market concerns about the sustainability of debt-fueled AI infrastructure growth.

items.title: Nvidia launches Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Bolt open models for enterprise agents and local AI on PCs [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Nvidia launches new open models to run agents in the enterprise and on PCs
items.summary:
Nvidia introduced new open-weight AI models designed for enterprise agents and edge computing, including the 120-billion-parameter Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for data center deployment and two lightweight Bolt models for local use on AI PCs and workstations. The Super VL model aims to deliver high accuracy and faster task completion compared to competitors, while the Bolt models target consumer and enterprise users seeking private, on-device AI assistants.

The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL supports tasks like document intelligence, financial accounting, and security resilience, and is already used by companies such as Skydance, EY, and Salesforce. Nvidia emphasizes that these open models allow organizations to post-train on their own data and deploy on their own infrastructure, contrasting with closed proprietary models. The Bolt models, compatible with Nvidia's RTX Spark chips, enable AI agents to run locally on PCs, addressing privacy concerns by avoiding cloud processing.

items.originalTitle: New paper: Emerging trends in AI agent evaluation
items.source: AI as Normal Technology, current/canonical related feed
items.summary:
A new paper by researchers from Princeton and partner institutions examines the evolving landscape of AI agent evaluation, highlighting the complexity of assessing agent performance beyond benchmark scores. The study addresses challenges such as the high cost and engineering effort required for evaluation, difficulties in monitoring agent behavior at scale, and the need for more rigorous tools and benchmarks.

The paper emphasizes that evaluation must consider multiple levels, from technical capabilities to real-world human-agent interactions and institutional impacts. It calls for a broader research agenda involving diverse evaluators and interdisciplinary approaches to better understand how AI agents function in context and how they augment or automate human tasks. The authors provide recommendations to support evaluators, funders, and the public in navigating this expanding evaluation ecosystem.

items.title: Anthropic Readies Model That Reads Users' Intentions Better [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic Readies Model That Reads Users' Intentions Better
items.summary:
In the last month, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google have released more than a dozen new models. If you thought that pace was crazy, don’t expect things to slow down anytime soon.

Anthropic is preparing to release a new model that is better in its reasoning and intuition than the Anthropic models that are currently available commercially, according to a person who has used it. The unreleased model is especially good at discerning a person’s underlying intentions and goals even if they don’t give the model much information, such as explicitly stating those goals, the person said. 

For instance, a person might ask the model to fix a single bug, and the model might go off and instead identify the underlying class of problems that caused the bug and ask whether it should fix the whole class of problems, said the person who has used it.

The Anthropic model is also better at thinking outside of the box rather than regurgitating common sense advice or solutions, the person said. For instance, if a user asks for advice on how to invest in stocks, rather than providing generic advice like looking at price-to-earnings ratios, the model might come up with its own creative algorithms to predict future stock performance, the person said.

items.originalTitle: Pentagon’s Emil Michael Vows Export Controls if AI Labs Don’t Cooperate With Government
items.summary:
Emil Michael, a senior Department of Defense official and member of President Trump’s “super intelligence” task force, vowed in an interview to use a range of executive tools including export controls to check the behavior of AI companies if they don’t cooperate with the government, while comparing frontier labs calling for more regulation to drunk drivers who demand someone else pull them over.

Michael drew widespread attention as the Trump administration official leading a public feud with Anthropic, pushing for the Defense Department to label the AI company a supply chain risk after it refused to remove safety guardrails. Now, as one of the four senior administration officials leading the Super Intelligence Force that Trump announced this month, Michael is charged with serving as the government’s liaison to Anthropic and other AI companies to develop protocols for handling cyber breaches, hacks and other critical incidents.

Tech earnings season is back (yes, I know it feels like it never ends). items.title: Neocloud Shakeout Looms, and Nvidia Has a Lot to Lose [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Neocloud Shakeout Looms, and Nvidia Has a Lot to Lose
items.summary:
How many young AI cloud providers can the market, and Nvidia, support?

That’s one of the big questions after a week in which investors worried about the data center buildout and the risks that its unproven participants, known as neoclouds, are taking. Those risks include loading up on debt (CoreWeave) or trying to go public without much of a track record (Firmus and Nscale). Firmus abruptly pulled its public offering last week while shares of CoreWeave and its smaller rivals fell around 20%. The concerns even hit bigger AI cloud providers like Oracle.

Data center and neocloud executives told me there’s a limit to the number of AI cloud providers that can exist, even if Nvidia provides many of them with investment or backstops.

items.title: Why Upstart Banks May Have to Keep Raising Money
items.originalTitle: Why Upstart Banks May Have to Keep Raising Money
items.summary:
The Trump administration has opened the door for entrepreneurs to start new banks in the U.S., many funded by venture capital. But there’s a catch for fast-growing newcomers. 

Upstarts like Palmer Luckey’s Erebor Bank, as well as other new entrants like Openreserve and Augustus, will likely have to keep raising money as they grow to maintain the capital cushion they need to satisfy bank regulatory requirements. That’s a contrast to most startups, which use fresh venture money to pay for operating expenses and expand the business. 

Regulators require banks to maintain a capital cushion to absorb potential losses and protect depositors. That cushion is typically measured through a minimum tier 1 leverage ratio, which measures a bank’s capital relative to assets including cash, loans and investments. For instance, a bank subject to a 12% minimum tier 1 leverage ratio needs to maintain at least $12 in capital for every $100 in assets. 

As a bank attracts more deposits, its assets, such as loans, typically grow too, increasing the amount of capital it needs to meet that minimum ratio. Established banks can build up their capital through their profits, but newer banks that aren’t yet profitable have to rely instead on raising fresh equity from investors.

Startup banks have already been raising significant funding to get their businesses off the ground or as deposits grow. 

Erebor Bank is set to raise $1.5 billion in a fresh fundraising round at an $8 billion valuation before the investment, after launching with $625 million in committed capital in February. The fundraising comes as the bank has seen its deposits surge to $7 billion as of the end of September, up from $4 billion at the end of the prior quarter. 

Meanwhile, Openreserve, an a16z crypto-backed bank that raised $25 million in September, said it expects to announce an additional capital raise to meet its regulatory requirements ahead of its planned opening early next year. 

Then there’s Augustus, a startup bank focused on serving fintech companies. It raised $180 million in a Tiger Global Management–led round in July at a $1 billion valuation and expects to open later this year. 

Regulators give capital ratios to each bank based on their assessment of the institution’s business plans and risks. Newly created banks typically face tougher capital requirements than established banks. For the first three years of operation, Erebor and Openreserve must each maintain a minimum tier 1 leverage ratio of 12%, while Augustus faces a 10% minimum. Established banks, by comparison, typically have ratios of between 5% and 6%. 

“There’s no question that the regulators treat de novo banks—new banks—differently than they do well-established banks,” according to Brian Graham, a partner and co-founder at consulting firm Klaros Group who advises clients on bank charter applications. Graham noted that the extra capital requirements typically go away after a bank has been operating for three years.

The upstart banks are generally pursuing relatively new business models or focusing on sectors big banks typically avoid. Erebor Bank, for example, has gained traction in areas prioritized by the Trump administration, such as defense startups and crypto firms, and is expanding in geographies traditional banks typically avoid, including Venezuela and Syria. 

In addition to making minimum capital requirements, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.—a banking regulator—imposed an unusual condition on its approval of Erebor for the deposit insurance program. Under a capital-call provision, Erebor’s investors must contribute additional capital if the bank doesn’t meet its minimum capital requirements, according to a filing. The filing didn’t disclose which investors are required to provide the capital backstop. 

In the meantime, upstart banks that are looking to drive revenue growth from lending rather than fees will likely need to tap investors to build their capital. 

“To the extent the bank’s business model is reliant materially on the balance sheet for revenue and net income, you’re going to need to raise more capital to drive growth,” Klaros’ Graham said. 

Openreserve, for its part, plans to make loans backed by traditional assets and turn them into digital tokens that can trade on blockchain, potentially providing a new source of loans for investors and lenders in the crypto market. For example, it plans to lend businesses money against their trade receivables, turning those assets into digital tokens to make them easier to trade. 

“Our ambition is to be the on-chain GSIB,” referring to a globally systemically important bank, said Dee Choubey, founder and CEO of Openreserve. The bank also plans to issue its own stablecoin and to offer tokenized deposits, digital versions of traditional bank accounts that earn interest. Over time, it aims to provide banking and payment services to other digital banks. 

Augustus plans to focus on helping fintech, crypto and remittance companies move money across borders using both traditional banking systems and stablecoins. That will put it in competition with existing banks like United Texas Bank, which has become dominant in processing dollar payments for overseas crypto exchanges.

“Whenever someone outside the U.S. touches the dollar through a local bank or local fintech, that always has to be facilitated by a U.S. nationally chartered clearing bank, so we provide that service,” said Augustus CEO Ferdinand Dabitz. In Europe, the bank already counts crypto exchange Kraken among its clients. 

Augustus is less focused on activities like lending, however, and has a lower ratio than the other two. The company has raised significantly more than its initial capital requirement, which could lessen the need for more fundraising in the near term. “We are less focused on the credit side as other market participants. We think the clearing side is really where we shine,” Dabitz said.

Augustus is less focused on activities like lending, however, and has a lower ratio than the other two. The company has raised significantly more than its initial capital requirement, which could lessen the need for more fundraising in the near term. “We are less focused on the credit side as other market participants. We think the clearing side is really where we shine,” Dabitz said.

items.title: Your Office Isn’t Spy Proof [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Your Office Isn’t Spy Proof
items.summary:
Welcome, Weekenders!

A song has been stuck on loop in my mind for days now. Yeah, this one. 

C’mon, haven’t you heard the big, brassy James Bond theme playing too? We have an honest-to-goodness spy scandal on our hands! That would be the affair over at OpenAI, where the FBI has arrested a former engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, for allegedly placing a toilet paper–wrapped recording device in a conference room. Why’d he do it? The Justice Department wasn’t explicit in its press release announcing Alfozan’s arrest, though the statement does make sure to prominently describe him as a “national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” implying, obviously, that he was hoping to spy on OpenAI for the Saudis.

I expect a not unsizable part of Silicon Valley experienced some schadenfreude when reading about the turn of events at OpenAI. I’d advise against indulging in that feeling, because when I struck up conversations with a few corporate security consultants and surveillance experts over the last few days, they all echoed the same sentiment: Plenty of companies risk ending up in the same situation—especially as they move quickly in today’s era of frenzied, heightened competition. A discomforting thought, eh?

“Organizations can sometimes be moving so fast that they often don’t understand that there’s an issue associated with somebody until that person’s on board and up to no good,” said Bill Priestap, a former head of FBI counterintelligence who now runs his own security consultancy, Trenchcoat Advisors. “Meaning they’re recruiting, and they’re under such pressure to get the right people and get them on board that in many regards, they end up with a minimal understanding of the people they’re bringing on board.” Well, good thing there hasn’t been an enormous, frantic hiring binge lately. Ha ha ha. 

If you’re starting to feel a little paranoid, I strongly, strongly advise against talking to someone like David Abbott, a San Francisco private detective, to find out how easy it is to bug an office. Such conversations will only further unnerve you—you might end up holding your next board meeting in your home basement, Tony Soprano style—because according to Abbott, it’s pretty darn easy to install a recording device. 

A suitable one can be bought for less than $100. Some of the popular ones resemble phone chargers, which get tucked into a power socket, hidden in plain sight. He’s also seen surveillance devices in fake coffee cups—you know, like the ones that might lie casually around an office—and quite a few in fake smoke alarms. 

More bad news: Should you find such a device, it’s like spotting an ant in your kitchen. One ant suggests the presence of more ants. “If I’m doing a bug sweep, just because I find one does not mean there isn’t a second,” said Abbott. “If you find one, there’s going to be two. If you find two, there’s going to be three. You just keep looking.”

What happened at OpenAI underscores Abbott’s warning. There, Alfozan, the alleged spy, did plant two bugs. Well, he tried to do so. Alfozan, not the sort who seems like he would’ve ever earned double 0 status, had placed another bug in a bag that he then mislaid: He reported it missing and had to go pick it up from the company’s lost and found.

OK, if I’ve spooked the heck out of you, I guess I can offer some solace by pointing you in the direction of Eric and Greg Levesque, whose Salt Lake City–based startup, Strider Technologies, has raised $110 million in the last few years to sell AI-powered software to businesses that monitors email and other internal communications, flagging suspicious behavior and possible espionage attempts. (Yes, the company’s name is a reference to Strider from “The Lord of the Rings,” the nom de cloak of Aragorn, the character Viggo Mortensen plays.) 

“What we’ve found is that companies are not always dealing with trained intelligence operatives. Like, they’re dealing with scientists or legitimate engineers who have been approached or coerced in some form or fashion and are now working on behalf of someone else,” said Greg Levesque. “They can leave a lot of digital exhaust.”—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

Listening: “Reaching Out”

As the pandemic shut down the world in 2020, Sayre Quevedo, then a producer for The New York Times’ “The Daily” podcast, quit his job and headed out to Los Angeles, hoping for a chance at self-reinvention. To cope with those tumultuous times, he decided to pursue a documentary project, recording every phone call. Had nothing else of import happened in his life, Quevedo might’ve wound up with an intriguing time capsule. But something quite unusual did occur: Just months after moving to LA, he and his twin brother, Connor, happened to finally locate their biological father, whom they’d never before met. He worked as a barber—blocks from where Sayre lived. “Reaching Out,” a new podcast co-produced by NPR station KCRW that won a top prize in the Tribeca Festival’s expanded podcast categories, is a starkly intimate account of their journey to meet him and their reconciliation with each other, their lives and what life might’ve been like if their father hadn’t been a total stranger who happened to be just down the street.—Abram Brown

Reading: “Sitcom” by Chuck Lorre and “Emperor of Nothing” by Blake J. Harris

Chuck Lorre, the indefatigable TV showrunner, writer and producer, has kept the masses laughing for years—and years—and years, with a list of hits that includes “Two and a Half Men,” “The Big Bang Theory” and “Dharma and Greg.” Those are sitcoms, a term Lorre acknowledges once made him practically break out in hives, since it was often used to cheapen what he sees as grueling, high-touch art. With spicy good humor, he reclaims the word in his new memoir about his time in Hollywood, “Sitcom.” 

“The truth is, making a live studio audience laugh for twenty-odd minutes every week, for twenty-two weeks, is incredibly hard and unbelievably stressful,” Lorre writes. “If you’re one of those people who insist on labeling all sitcoms as being cheap, juvenile and unsophisticated, well...all I can say is, blow me.”

I’d say “Sitcom” functions as a good primer on managing talent, too, and Lorre attests to having learned the importance of keeping out of the way. “Creativity needs air to breathe,” he writes. To do the opposite risks turning a leader into “one of those plastic bags you get at the dry cleaners that can kill small children.” Lorre also takes the opportunity to set down what he sees as good comedy’s basic tenets and decry the medium’s basest impulse: to write only about stupid people doing stupid things: “A better, perhaps deeper means to achieving laughter involves pain and suffering.”

Such a sentiment is most certainly shared by Larry David of “Seinfeld” and “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” the subject of “Emperor of Nothing,” a biography that won his reluctant cooperation. (When author Blake J. Harris finally wore David down, Harris received a two-line email from him: “Oh Jesus. If we must.”) As with “Sitcom,” “Emperor of Nothing” charts a remarkable rise across Hollywood from an inauspicious start: Lorre was a wannabe musician before his TV run, while David was a little-known stand-up comic with an unremarkable series of TV writing jobs before co-creating “Seinfeld.”

Like Lorre, David describes the process of penning comedy as an arduous affair. And by David’s own telling, the process of sitting down to write a new “Seinfeld” season would bring on full panic. “That always seemed like a daunting prospect,” he recalled. “Especially because all the good ideas were used up the year before.” Fortunately, David had his friendship with the show’s eponymous star, Jerry Seinfeld, one of many people within David’s orbit who gave interviews for “Emperor of Nothing.” “I would always say, ‘All we have to do is write today,’” Seinfeld said. Or as David recalled: “Jerry always talked me off the ledge.”—A.B.

Watching: “War”

No one does a charming, self-involved cad better than Dominic West, the British character actor who first washed ashore in America as “The Wire”’s Detective McNulty and then again in Showtime’s “The Affair” and in the final two seasons of “The Crown” as Prince Charles. In “War,” HBO’s new high-tension legal drama, he’s tech billionaire Morgan Henderson, a fellow championing a safer, more responsible social media—while embroiled in an increasingly messy divorce from his Hollywood star wife, Carla (Sienna Miller). Much of that mess is Morgan’s own doing: He looks wonderful in his Savile Row trousers—he just has trouble keeping them on. As Morgan and Carla gird for an extended battle, they assemble a posse of cutthroat attorneys, who find their impulsive clients constantly upending their carefully laid strategies. That flock of legal eagles includes a handsome rogue, Johnny (Archie Renaux), a lad from working-class south London who sees a chance to ascend by, uh, redefining zealous representation. Backstabbing and double crosses abound.—A.B.

Had nothing else of import happened in his life, Quevedo might’ve wound up with an intriguing time capsule. But something quite unusual did occur: Just months after moving to LA, he and his twin brother, Connor, happened to finally locate their biological father, whom they’d never before met. He worked as a barber—blocks from where Sayre lived. “Reaching Out,” a new podcast co-produced by NPR station KCRW that won a top prize in the Tribeca Festival’s expanded podcast categories, is a starkly intimate account of their journey to meet him and their reconciliation with each other, their lives and what life might’ve been like if their father hadn’t been a total stranger who happened to be just down the street.—Abram Brown

Reading: “Sitcom” by Chuck Lorre and “Emperor of Nothing” by Blake J. Harris

Chuck Lorre, the indefatigable TV showrunner, writer and producer, has kept the masses laughing for years—and years—and years, with a list of hits that includes “Two and a Half Men,” “The Big Bang Theory” and “Dharma and Greg.” Those are sitcoms, a term Lorre acknowledges once made him practically break out in hives, since it was often used to cheapen what he sees as grueling, high-touch art. With spicy good humor, he reclaims the word in his new memoir about his time in Hollywood, “Sitcom.” 

“The truth is, making a live studio audience laugh for twenty-odd minutes every week, for twenty-two weeks, is incredibly hard and unbelievably stressful,” Lorre writes. “If you’re one of those people who insist on labeling all sitcoms as being cheap, juvenile and unsophisticated, well...all I can say is, blow me.”

I’d say “Sitcom” functions as a good primer on managing talent, too, and Lorre attests to having learned the importance of keeping out of the way. “Creativity needs air to breathe,” he writes. To do the opposite risks turning a leader into “one of those plastic bags you get at the dry cleaners that can kill small children.” Lorre also takes the opportunity to set down what he sees as good comedy’s basic tenets and decry the medium’s basest impulse: to write only about stupid people doing stupid things: “A better, perhaps deeper means to achieving laughter involves pain and suffering.”

Such a sentiment is most certainly shared by Larry David of “Seinfeld” and “Curb Your Enthusiasm,” the subject of “Emperor of Nothing,” a biography that won his reluctant cooperation. (When author Blake J. Harris finally wore David down, Harris received a two-line email from him: “Oh Jesus. If we must.”) As with “Sitcom,” “Emperor of Nothing” charts a remarkable rise across Hollywood from an inauspicious start: Lorre was a wannabe musician before his TV run, while David was a little-known stand-up comic with an unremarkable series of TV writing jobs before co-creating “Seinfeld.”

Like Lorre, David describes the process of penning comedy as an arduous affair. And by David’s own telling, the process of sitting down to write a new “Seinfeld” season would bring on full panic. “That always seemed like a daunting prospect,” he recalled. “Especially because all the good ideas were used up the year before.” Fortunately, David had his friendship with the show’s eponymous star, Jerry Seinfeld, one of many people within David’s orbit who gave interviews for “Emperor of Nothing.” “I would always say, ‘All we have to do is write today,’” Seinfeld said. Or as David recalled: “Jerry always talked me off the ledge.”—A.B.

Watching: “War”

No one does a charming, self-involved cad better than Dominic West, the British character actor who first washed ashore in America as “The Wire”’s Detective McNulty and then again in Showtime’s “The Affair” and in the final two seasons of “The Crown” as Prince Charles. In “War,” HBO’s new high-tension legal drama, he’s tech billionaire Morgan Henderson, a fellow championing a safer, more responsible social media—while embroiled in an increasingly messy divorce from his Hollywood star wife, Carla (Sienna Miller). Much of that mess is Morgan’s own doing: He looks wonderful in his Savile Row trousers—he just has trouble keeping them on. As Morgan and Carla gird for an extended battle, they assemble a posse of cutthroat attorneys, who find their impulsive clients constantly upending their carefully laid strategies. That flock of legal eagles includes a handsome rogue, Johnny (Archie Renaux), a lad from working-class south London who sees a chance to ascend by, uh, redefining zealous representation. Backstabbing and double crosses abound.—A.B.
